title: Next Permutation
statement:
Rearrange the integer array `nums` into the arrangement that comes right after it when all orderings of its values are listed in lexicographic (dictionary) order. If `nums` is already the largest such ordering, rearrange it into the smallest one instead, which is ascending order.

Duplicate values are allowed, and orderings that are identical as sequences count once. Modify `nums` in place using only O(1) extra memory and return nothing.
notes:
## Intuition

Listing every ordering and picking the one after `nums` takes factorial time. Instead, think of the array as a number to increase by the smallest step. The longest non-increasing run at the right end is already as large as it can be, so the change must happen just before it, at the **pivot**. Swap the pivot with the smallest larger value in that run, then make the run as small as possible.

## Approach

1. Walk `pivot` leftward from the second-to-last index while `nums[pivot] >= nums[pivot + 1]`. Everything to its right is then non-increasing.
2. If a pivot exists, scan `successor` from the right end until `nums[successor] > nums[pivot]`; because the run is non-increasing, this is the smallest value larger than the pivot. Swap the two.
3. The run after the pivot is still non-increasing, so reversing it with `left` and `right` pointers sorts it ascending.
4. If no pivot exists (`pivot = -1`), step 3 reverses the whole array, giving the smallest ordering.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3]`. `pivot` starts at 1, and `2 < 3`, so the pivot stays at index 1. `successor` starts at index 2, and `3 > 2`, so swap: `[1, 3, 2]`. The run after the pivot is just `[2]` (`left = right = 2`), so the reversal does nothing. The result is `[1, 3, 2]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each of the three scans moves across the array at most once.
- Space: O(1): only a few indices; all swaps happen inside `nums`.

## Pitfalls

- Use `>=` when finding the pivot and `<=` when finding the successor, or duplicates such as `[1, 5, 1]` break the result.
- Reverse the suffix, do not sort it: it is already in descending order, so reversing is O(n).
- When there is no pivot, still reverse the whole array; do not return early with the input unchanged.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pivot` | last index whose value is smaller than the next one, or -1 |
| `successor` | rightmost index whose value is larger than `nums[pivot]` |
| `left`, `right` | ends of the suffix being reversed |

narration.2: Start the pivot search at the second-to-last index.
narration.3: Move left while the value does not rise toward the next one; that suffix cannot get any larger.
narration.6: A pivot exists only if some value is smaller than its right neighbour.
narration.7: Search for the swap partner from the right end.
narration.8: Skip values that are not strictly larger than the pivot.
narration.11: Swap the pivot with the smallest larger value to its right.
narration.13: The suffix to reverse starts just after the pivot (index 0 when there is no pivot)...
narration.15: The suffix is non-increasing, so reversing it makes it ascending.
narration.16: Swap the two ends of the suffix.
